level1.text: The vibrating part of the lowest string of a double bass is $1.05\,\text{m}$ long, and a wave travels in the string at the speed $86.1\,\text{m/s}$. The string is fixed at both ends. What is the fundamental frequency of the string?

In a school project a pipe open at both ends is made from a plastic tube whose length is $0.330\,\text{m}$. What is the fundamental frequency of the air column of the tube? Use $340\,\text{m/s}$ as the speed of sound in air.
The largest pipe of a church organ is closed at its upper end and its length is $2.60\,\text{m}$. What is the fundamental frequency of the pipe? Use $340\,\text{m/s}$ as the speed of sound in air.

In a PE lesson a long rope fixed to a wall is shaken so that a standing wave forms in it. The distance between two adjacent nodes is measured to be $0.35\,\text{m}$. What is the wavelength of the waves travelling in the rope?
The fundamental frequency of the G string of a cello is $98.0\,\text{Hz}$. What is the fourth natural frequency of the string, that is, the frequency at which four antinodes fit on the string?
A standing wave has formed in a guitar string. Which of the following describes an antinode of the string correctly?
level1.answer: A point where the string vibrates with the greatest amplitude, because the waves are always in the same phase there.

choices.text: A point where the string stays still all the time, because waves travelling in opposite directions cancel each other there.
choices.feedback: This describes a node, not an antinode. At a node the waves travelling in opposite directions are in opposite phases at every moment and the displacement is zero.

choices.text: A point where the string vibrates with the greatest amplitude, because the waves are always in the same phase there.
choices.feedback: Correct: at an antinode the waves travelling in opposite directions are in the same phase at every moment and reinforce each other, so the amplitude is greatest. An antinode is halfway between two nodes.

choices.text: A point to which a wave crest travels along the string, because a standing wave carries crests from one end of the string to the other.
choices.feedback: In a standing wave a wave crest does not travel. An antinode is a fixed point of the string where the string vibrates up and down, and the crests stay in the same places.

choices.text: A point where the string is fixed, because at the fixing point the string moves the most and reflects the wave back.
choices.feedback: At the fixing point the string cannot move, so there is a node. The reflection occurs precisely because the fixing point stays still.

level1.text: The fundamental frequency of a tube closed at one end is $150\,\text{Hz}$. Which of the following is also a natural frequency of the tube?
level1.answer: $450\,\text{Hz}$, because the natural frequencies are odd multiples of the fundamental frequency.

choices.text: $300\,\text{Hz}$, because the natural frequencies are all whole-number multiples of the fundamental frequency, as for a string.
choices.feedback: This is true for a string fixed at both ends and for a tube open at both ends. A closed tube has a node at one end and an antinode at the other, so $2 f_1$ is not a natural frequency.

choices.text: $450\,\text{Hz}$, because the natural frequencies are odd multiples of the fundamental frequency.
choices.feedback: Correct: the length of a closed tube is an odd number of quarter wavelengths, so the natural frequencies are $f_1$, $3 f_1$, $5 f_1$ and so on. Here $3 f_1 = 450\,\text{Hz}$.

choices.text: $600\,\text{Hz}$, because the natural frequencies of a closed tube are multiples of four of the fundamental frequency.
choices.feedback: The four belongs in the formula $f_1 = \tfrac{v}{4L}$, but the factor $n$ is odd, because the natural frequencies are $f_n = n f_1$. The number $600\,\text{Hz} = 4 f_1$ is not one.

choices.text: $75\,\text{Hz}$, because lower natural frequencies are obtained by dividing the fundamental frequency by a whole number.
choices.feedback: The fundamental frequency is the lowest natural frequency, so there is no lower one. The other natural frequencies are higher than the fundamental frequency.

level1.text:
A student is solving the problem: “The vibrating part of a guitar string is $0.60\,\text{m}$ long and the speed of the wave in the string is $120\,\text{m/s}$. What is the fundamental frequency of the string?” The student writes: “At the fundamental frequency one wavelength fits on the string, so $\lambda = L = 0.60\,\text{m}$ and therefore $f = 200\,\text{Hz}$.” The string is fixed at both ends.

a) What is the error in the student's reasoning?

b) Calculate the fundamental frequency of the string correctly.

The answer box takes the result of part b).

An open-open pipe (open at both ends) is $0.50\,\text{m}$ long. The pipe is filled first with helium and then with air, and the temperature of both gases is $0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. Look up the speed of sound in each gas in the MAFY table (mafytaulukot.fi). By how many hertz is the fundamental frequency of the pipe higher with helium than with air?
hints: The values are found in the MAFY table under *Aaltoliike* (wave motion), in the table *Äänen nopeuksia eri väliaineissa* (speeds of sound in different media).

level2.text: The vibrating part of a guitar string is $0.650\,\text{m}$ long. When the guitarist tightens the string with the tuning peg, the speed of the wave in the string increases from $141.0\,\text{m/s}$ to $148.0\,\text{m/s}$. By how many hertz does the fundamental frequency of the string rise?

The speed of sound is measured with a resonance tube. The lower part of a vertical tube contains water, and a tuning fork with the frequency $440\,\text{Hz}$ sounds above the upper end of the tube.

When the water level is lowered, the sound is amplified for the first time when the air column from the water surface to the mouth of the tube is $19.3\,\text{cm}$ long. The water surface acts as the closed end of the tube.

What is the speed of sound in air according to the measurement?
The third natural frequency of a tube open at both ends is $1530\,\text{Hz}$. How long is the tube? Use $340\,\text{m/s}$ as the speed of sound in air. Give the answer in centimetres.

In the figure a vibrator vibrates at the frequency $100\,\text{Hz}$, and the rope between the vibrator and the pulley vibrates as a standing wave. The positions of the vibrator and the pulley are nodes. What is the speed of the wave in the rope? Read the necessary data from the figure.

The vibrating part of a guitar string is $0.640\,\text{m}$ long, and the string is fixed at both ends. A vibrator is used to find the frequencies at which the string resonates, and at each resonance the number $n$ of antinodes visible on the string is counted. The table shows the measurement results (example data).

Determine the speed of the wave in the string from the data. First calculate $\tfrac{f}{n}$ for each row and take their mean $f_{1,\text{av}}$.

level2.text:
The speed of sound is measured with a resonance tube. The lower part of a vertical tube contains water, and a tuning fork with the frequency $512\,\text{Hz}$ sounds above the mouth of the tube. When the water level is lowered, the sound is amplified at three points. The water surface acts as the closed end of the tube. The table shows the length $L$ of the air column from the water surface to the mouth of the tube at each point (example data).

a) Determine the speed of sound in air. Use the difference between the lengths of the first and the third resonance, in which case the end correction of the tube is not needed.

b) Calculate how much the first length deviates from a quarter of a wavelength, and explain the cause of the deviation.

The answer box takes the result of part a).

data.caption: Resonances of the tuning fork $512\,\text{Hz}$ (example data)

level2.text: A guitarist presses the string against the fingerboard with a finger, and the pitch of the string rises. The tension of the string does not change when it is pressed. Which of the following explains the rise in pitch?
level2.answer: The vibrating part becomes shorter, so the wavelength decreases and the frequency increases when the speed of the wave does not change.

choices.text: The speed of the wave in the string increases, because a wave can travel faster in a shorter string.
choices.feedback: The speed of the wave in a string depends on the tension and the thickness of the string, not on its length. The tension and the thickness do not change, so the speed stays the same.

choices.text: The wavelength stays the same, because it depends only on the speed of the wave, and the frequency increases because of the shorter string.
choices.feedback: At the fundamental frequency $\lambda = 2L$, so the wavelength becomes shorter with the string. If the wavelength stayed the same and the speed stayed the same, the frequency would not change either.

choices.text: The vibrating part becomes shorter, so the wavelength decreases and the frequency increases when the speed of the wave does not change.
choices.feedback: Correct: at the fundamental frequency $\lambda = 2L$ and $v = f\lambda$. When $L$ decreases and $v$ stays the same, $\lambda$ decreases and $f = \tfrac{v}{2L}$ increases.

choices.text: The amplitude of the string increases when it is shortened, so the wave travels faster and the frequency increases.
choices.feedback: The amplitude determines neither the speed of the wave nor the frequency. The speed of the wave depends on the string, and the frequency is determined by the speed and the length of the vibrating part.

level2.text:
An organ builder makes two pipes from the same tube. The first pipe is open at both ends and its length is $L$. The second pipe is half as long, $\tfrac{L}{2}$, and its upper end is closed with a plug. The air temperature is the same, and the end correction of the pipe is ignored.

How does the fundamental frequency of the second pipe change compared with the fundamental frequency of the first pipe?
level2.answer: The fundamental frequency stays the same.

choices.feedback: Here the closed pipe has been calculated like an open pipe or a string, so only the halving of the length matters. In a closed pipe only a quarter of a wavelength fits into the length at the fundamental frequency, so $f_1 = \tfrac{v}{4L}$ and not $\tfrac{v}{2L}$.

choices.text: The fundamental frequency stays the same.
choices.feedback: Correct: halving the length doubles the fundamental frequency, and the closed end halves it. The fundamental frequency of the second pipe is $\tfrac{v}{4 \cdot L/2} = \tfrac{v}{2L}$, that is, the same as that of the first pipe.

choices.text: The fundamental frequency drops to half.
choices.feedback: Here only the plug has been taken into account, which halves the fundamental frequency of a pipe of the same length. However, the pipe is also half as long, and a shorter pipe sounds higher, so the changes cancel each other.

choices.text: The fundamental frequency becomes four times as high.
choices.feedback: Here the effect of the plug has been read the wrong way round. The fundamental frequency of a closed pipe is $\tfrac{v}{4L}$, so the plug halves the fundamental frequency and does not double it. Only halving the length doubles the fundamental frequency.

level2.text: In the rope in the figure the speed of the wave is $75.0\,\text{m/s}$. The rope between the vibrator and the pulley vibrates as a standing wave, and the positions of the vibrator and the pulley are nodes. The vibrator's frequency is now such that the rope vibrates in the four-loop pattern of the figure. By how many hertz must the frequency be raised so that the rope has five loops? Read the necessary data from the figure.

level3.text: The fundamental frequency of an organ pipe open at both ends is $262\,\text{Hz}$. The organ builder closes the upper end of the pipe with a plug. What is the new fundamental frequency of the pipe? The length of the pipe and the temperature of the air do not change.

A string fixed at both ends is driven by a vibrator whose frequency can be adjusted. When the frequency is raised, the string resonates strongly at the frequency $330\,\text{Hz}$ and the next time at $440\,\text{Hz}$, but at no frequency between them. What is the fundamental frequency of the string?

A loudspeaker whose frequency is varied sounds near the mouth of a tube closed at one end. The tube resonates at the frequencies $510\,\text{Hz}$ and $850\,\text{Hz}$, but at no frequency between them. How long is the tube? Use $340\,\text{m/s}$ as the speed of sound in air.

The vibrating part of a guitar string is $0.650\,\text{m}$ long in all the measurements, and the string is fixed at both ends. The tension $F$ of the string is changed with the tuning peg, and the fundamental frequency $f_1$ of the string is measured at each tension. The table shows the measurement results (example data).

We investigate whether the fundamental frequency is proportional to the square root of the tension, $f_1 \propto \sqrt{F}$, or to the tension itself, $f_1 \propto F$.

a) Calculate the ratios $\tfrac{f_1}{F}$ and $\tfrac{f_1^2}{F}$ for each measurement. Which ratio stays constant within the measurement uncertainty?

b) Based on part a), deduce by what factor the fundamental frequency changes when the tension is quadrupled.

c) Predict the fundamental frequency when the tension is $120\,\text{N}$. Use the mean of the ratio $\tfrac{f_1^2}{F}$ as the constant and evaluate the reliability of the prediction.

The answer box takes the result of part c).

data.caption: Fundamental frequency of a string at different tensions (example data)

level3.text:
In a cold warehouse two tubes A and B of the same length, $0.800\,\text{m}$, are investigated. One is open at both ends and the other is closed at one end, but the labels have been lost. A loudspeaker whose frequency is raised sounds near the mouth of the tube, and the three lowest resonance frequencies are measured. The end correction of the tube is ignored. The speed of sound in the warehouse is not $340\,\text{m/s}$, because the air is cold. The table shows the measurement results (example data).

a) Deduce from the ratios of the frequencies which tube is open and which is closed.

b) Calculate the speed of sound in air from the results of both tubes and give their mean as the final result.

c) Explain why the tubes sound different although they are equally long.

The answer box takes the mean of part b).

data.caption: Resonance frequencies of the tubes (example data)
